title: Online Social Networking and Addiction—A Review of the Psychological Literature
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
abstract: Social Networking Sites (SNSs) are virtual communities where users can create individual public profiles, interact with real-life friends, and meet other people based on shared interests. They are seen as a 'global consumer phenomenon' with an exponential rise in usage within the last few years. Anecdotal case study evidence suggests that 'addiction' to social networks on the Internet may be a potential mental health problem for some users. However, the contemporary scientific literature addressing the addictive qualities of social networks on the Internet is scarce. Therefore, this literature review is intended to provide empirical and conceptual insight into the emerging phenomenon of addiction to SNSs by: (1) outlining SNS usage patterns, (2) examining motivations for SNS usage, (3) examining personalities of SNS users, (4) examining negative consequences of SNS usage, (5) exploring potential SNS addiction, and (6) exploring SNS addiction specificity and comorbidity. The findings indicate that SNSs are predominantly used for social purposes, mostly related to the maintenance of established offline networks. Moreover, extraverts appear to use social networking sites for social enhancement, whereas introverts use it for social compensation, each of which appears to be related to greater usage, as does low conscientiousness and high narcissism. Negative correlates of SNS usage include the decrease in real life social community participation and academic achievement, as well as relationship problems, each of which may be indicative of potential addiction.

claims.text: High extraversion significantly predicts addictive tendencies toward social networking sites.
Low conscientiousness significantly predicts addictive tendencies toward social networking sites.
Social searching on Facebook produces higher emotional pleasure than social browsing as measured by psychophysiological metrics.
Facebook users have lower Grade Point Averages compared to non-users among university students.
Facebook users spend less time studying compared to non-users among university students.
24% of surveyed Chinese college students met the threshold for addiction to the social networking game Happy Farm using the Internet Addiction Test.
34% of surveyed Chinese college students met the classification for addiction to Xiaonei.com using Young's Internet Addiction Test.

limitations.text: Existing empirical studies rely heavily on small, non-representative convenience samples of university students and teenagers, severely limiting generalizability.
The existing scientific literature lacks longitudinal designs, preventing any causal inferences between excessive SNS usage and reported negative consequences.
Quantitative studies in prior literature measure general addictive tendencies or high-frequency usage rather than establishing clinical addiction pathology and impairment.

future_work.text: Conduct longitudinal studies to determine causal relationships between heavy SNS usage and functional negative correlates.
Utilize larger, nationally representative samples across varied age groups to improve external validity.
Apply validated and diagnostic clinical criteria adapted from DSM or ICD manuals to differentiate true addiction from high-frequency or excessive use.
Investigate SNS addiction specificity and potential comorbidities with substance use disorders and other behavioral addictions.

methodologies.name: Systematic Narrative Literature Review
methodologies.description: A comprehensive narrative review evaluating 43 empirical studies extracted from Web of Knowledge and Google Scholar covering usage, motivations, personality, negative consequences, addiction, and comorbidity in SNS contexts.
conditions: Studies addressing SNS usage, motivations, personality traits, negative correlates, addiction, or comorbidity
